questiontext.text: In the Model Mutation Explorer, mutation operators are applied to:

answer.text: A behavioural model (here a Mealy FSM: its transitions, next-states and outputs), not the program's source code

feedback.text: Correct — model mutation edits the FSM, leaving code and tests unchanged.

answer.text: The program's source code

feedback.text: Editing source code is code-level (program) mutation, a different technique.

answer.text: The test suite's input sequences

feedback.text: The suite is what we run against the mutants; the operator changes the model.

answer.text: The output traces produced by the suite

feedback.text: Traces are computed results, not the artifact that is mutated.

generalfeedback.text: Model mutation seeds one small change into the model (an FSM) — a transition, its target state, or its output — rather than into the code.

questiontext.text: A model-mutant in the explorer is:

answer.text: A copy of the base FSM with exactly one mutation operator applied (e.g. one transition deleted or retargeted)

feedback.text: Correct — one operator makes one small change to the base model.

answer.text: A copy of the base FSM with every transition changed at once

feedback.text: A mutant carries a single deliberate change, not many.

answer.text: A test case that fails on the base model

feedback.text: That is a test, not a mutated model.

answer.text: A second FSM designed independently from scratch

feedback.text: A mutant is derived from the base by one operator, not written anew.

generalfeedback.text: Each mutant (M1–M5) is the base FSM with one operator applied: delete a transition, retarget it, or change its output.

questiontext.text: A model-mutant is killed when:

answer.text: Some test's output trace on the mutant differs from its output trace on the base model

feedback.text: Correct — a distinguishing output trace kills the mutant.

answer.text: The mutant FSM has fewer states than the base

feedback.text: State count does not decide killing; a differing trace does.

answer.text: The mutant fails to load

feedback.text: Killing is about distinguishing behaviour, not loading.

answer.text: The mutant produces the same output trace as the base on every test

feedback.text: That is the definition of surviving, not of being killed.

generalfeedback.text: A killing test is one whose output trace on the mutant differs from the base — that observable difference is what "kills" the mutant.

questiontext.text: How does model mutation differ from I-series code (program) mutation?

answer.text: Model mutation edits the FSM/model; code mutation edits the program source

feedback.text: Correct — the two differ in which artifact is mutated.

answer.text: Model mutation uses random inputs while code mutation is systematic

feedback.text: Both apply systematic operators; the difference is the mutated artifact.

answer.text: Model mutation needs no mutation operators

feedback.text: Both use operators; model mutation applies them to the model.

answer.text: They are the same technique under two names

feedback.text: They are distinct: one mutates a model, the other source code.

generalfeedback.text: Model mutation works at a higher abstraction — mutants are FSM edits, not source edits.

questiontext.text: Which is one of the model mutation operators used in the explorer?

answer.text: Retarget a transition (change its next state)

feedback.text: Correct — retarget is one of the three operators.

answer.text: Rename a C++ variable

feedback.text: That is a code-level change, not a model operator.

answer.text: Delete a source-code statement

feedback.text: Deleting source is code mutation, not model mutation.

answer.text: Insert a unary minus into a program expression

feedback.text: That is a code mutation operator (UOI), not a model operator.

generalfeedback.text: The explorer's three operators are: delete a transition, retarget a transition, and change a transition's output.

questiontext.text: The delete model mutation operator:

answer.text: Removes a transition, so on that input the mutant gets stuck and its trace shows ⊥

feedback.text: Correct — a deleted-transition mutant has no move for that input.

answer.text: Deletes an entire state and all of its transitions

feedback.text: The operator removes a single transition, not a whole state.

answer.text: Changes a transition's output symbol

feedback.text: That is the output operator, not delete.

answer.text: Redirects a transition to a different state

feedback.text: That is the retarget operator, not delete.

generalfeedback.text: Delete drops one transition; when a run needs it, the trace records ⊥ because no transition matches.

questiontext.text: The retarget operator changes:

answer.text: The next state (destination) a transition leads to

feedback.text: Correct — retarget changes where a transition goes.

answer.text: The output symbol a transition emits

feedback.text: That is the output operator.

answer.text: The input symbol that triggers a transition

feedback.text: The explorer's retarget changes the destination, not the trigger.

answer.text: The initial state of the FSM

feedback.text: Retarget alters a transition's target, not the initial state.

generalfeedback.text: Retarget (e.g. "Retarget q2a → state q1") points a transition at a new destination state while keeping its input and output.

questiontext.text: The output operator changes:

answer.text: The output symbol emitted on a transition (e.g. q1 on 'a' emits 1 instead of 0)

feedback.text: Correct — the output operator alters what a transition emits.

answer.text: The destination state of the transition

feedback.text: That is retarget, not the output operator.

answer.text: The input that triggers the transition

feedback.text: The output operator changes the emitted symbol, not the trigger.

answer.text: The number of states in the machine

feedback.text: No states are added or removed by the output operator.

generalfeedback.text: The output operator (e.g. "Change output of q1a → 1") replaces the symbol a transition emits, leaving its source, input and target unchanged.

questiontext.text: The base model is a Mealy machine. In a Mealy machine each output is associated with:

answer.text: A transition (an input taken in a state), so a run yields an output trace

feedback.text: Correct — Mealy outputs are on transitions.

answer.text: A state only

feedback.text: That describes a Moore machine, not the Mealy model used here.

answer.text: The whole machine, emitted once

feedback.text: Each transition emits an output; it is not a single machine-wide value.

answer.text: The final state only

feedback.text: Outputs appear on every transition along the run, not just at the end.

generalfeedback.text: In the Mealy FSM here, each transition carries an output symbol; running an input sequence produces the output trace the explorer compares.

questiontext.text: The model mutation score reported by the explorer measures:

answer.text: The fraction of model-mutants the suite kills — test adequacy at the model abstraction level

feedback.text: Correct — it is killed/total, a model-level adequacy measure.

answer.text: The number of states in the FSM

feedback.text: The score is about mutants killed, not state count.

answer.text: The runtime of the suite

feedback.text: Runtime is unrelated to the mutation score.

answer.text: The number of transitions that were mutated

feedback.text: The score is the proportion killed, not how many were mutated.

generalfeedback.text: The model mutation score is the proportion of model-mutants distinguished (killed) by the suite, gauging test adequacy at the model level.

questiontext.text: A model-mutant that survived means:

answer.text: Every test in the suite produced the same output trace on the mutant as on the base model

feedback.text: Correct — no test distinguished it.

answer.text: At least one test distinguished it from the base

feedback.text: That would make it killed, not a survivor.

answer.text: The mutant failed to parse

feedback.text: Surviving is about matching traces, not parsing.

answer.text: The base model is faulty

feedback.text: Surviving says nothing about the base being wrong.

generalfeedback.text: A survivor produced base-identical traces on every test — either a suite gap or an equivalent mutant.

questiontext.text: In an output trace, the symbol ⊥ indicates:

answer.text: A missing transition — the model had no move for that input in the current state, so the run got stuck

feedback.text: Correct — ⊥ marks a stuck run at a missing transition.

answer.text: The output symbol 0

feedback.text: 0 is a normal output; ⊥ specifically marks a missing transition.

answer.text: The end of the input sequence

feedback.text: ⊥ signals a stuck run, not the normal end of input.

answer.text: That the mutant is equivalent

feedback.text: ⊥ is unrelated to equivalence; it marks a missing transition.

generalfeedback.text: runTrace appends ⊥ when no transition matches the current state and input — a deleted-transition mutant gets stuck.

questiontext.text: An equivalent model-mutant is one that:

answer.text: Differs from the base model syntactically but behaves identically, so no test can ever kill it

feedback.text: Correct — identical behaviour makes it unkillable.

answer.text: Is textually identical to the base model

feedback.text: A mutant always makes a change; identical text is not a mutant.

answer.text: Is always killed by the first test

feedback.text: An equivalent mutant is never killed, by definition.

answer.text: Cannot be produced by any operator

feedback.text: It is produced by an operator; it just happens to preserve behaviour.

generalfeedback.text: An equivalent mutant is a real syntactic change that leaves behaviour unchanged (here q2a→q4, since q3 and q4 behave identically), so no test distinguishes it.

questiontext.text: Model mutation testing works by mutating the program's source code and running tests against it.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Mutating source code is code-level mutation. Model mutation changes the model (the FSM) instead.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — model mutation edits the FSM's transitions, targets and outputs, not the source code.

generalfeedback.text: Model mutation seeds changes into a behavioural model; mutating source code is the separate technique of program (code) mutation.

questiontext.text: In the explorer, each test in the suite is:

answer.text: An input sequence (a string of input symbols) fed to the model, yielding an output trace

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. "aa", "aba"; the run produces an output trace.

answer.text: A single output symbol

feedback.text: A test is a sequence of inputs, not one output.

answer.text: A whole mutant FSM

feedback.text: A mutant is a model; a test is an input sequence run on it.

answer.text: A state of the FSM

feedback.text: A test drives the FSM through states; it is not itself a state.

generalfeedback.text: The suite is a set of input strings (aa, ab, ba, aaa, aba); each is run to produce an output trace compared between base and mutant.

name.text: What test aa reveals for the delete mutant

questiontext.text: The mutant that deletes transition q2-a is killed by input aa. What does aa show?

answer.text: Base trace "01" vs mutant trace "0⊥": the mutant gets stuck when it needs q2-a

feedback.text: Correct — after q1-a emits 0 into q2, the deleted q2-a leaves the run stuck (⊥).

answer.text: Base "01" vs mutant "01": identical, so it is not killed

feedback.text: The mutant cannot take q2-a, so its trace is "0⊥", not "01".

answer.text: Both produce ⊥ immediately on the first input

feedback.text: The first input q1-a still works; ⊥ appears only at the second step.

answer.text: The mutant simply has one more state

feedback.text: Delete removes a transition, not adds a state; the trace difference is what kills it.

generalfeedback.text: On "aa" the base yields "01" but the delete-q2a mutant yields "0⊥"; the differing trace kills it.

questiontext.text: Changing q1-a's output from 0 to 1 is an instance of which operator?

answer.text: The output operator (change a transition's output symbol)

feedback.text: Correct — only the emitted symbol changed.

answer.text: The retarget operator

feedback.text: Retarget changes the destination state, not the output.

answer.text: The delete operator

feedback.text: Nothing was removed; the output was changed.

answer.text: Adding a new state

feedback.text: No state was added; this is an output change.

generalfeedback.text: Altering the symbol a transition emits (q1-a: 0→1) is the output operator — exactly mutant M3.

questiontext.text: Making transition q2-a lead to q1 instead of q3, with its output unchanged, is which operator?

answer.text: Retarget (change the transition's next state)

feedback.text: Correct — the destination changed while the output stayed the same.

answer.text: Output change

feedback.text: The output was not changed; the destination was.

answer.text: Delete

feedback.text: The transition still exists; only its target changed.

answer.text: Input-symbol change

feedback.text: The triggering input is unchanged; the target state changed.

generalfeedback.text: Redirecting q2-a to a new state is the retarget operator (mutant M2 sends it to q1).

name.text: Why the q3-b output mutant survives

questiontext.text: The mutant that changes q3-b's output to 0 survives the whole suite. Why?

answer.text: No test in the suite ever takes the q3-b transition, so the changed output is never observed — a suite gap, not equivalence

feedback.text: Correct — aa, ab, ba, aaa, aba never take b from q3.

answer.text: Because q3-b's output can never be observed in principle (an equivalent mutant)

feedback.text: It is not equivalent: a test reaching q3 then taking b would kill it.

answer.text: Because changing an output never changes any trace

feedback.text: Output changes do change traces — when the transition is exercised.

answer.text: Because the base model is wrong

feedback.text: The base is fine; the suite simply misses q3-b.

generalfeedback.text: The suite leaves q3-b uncovered, so the mutation is never triggered — a fixable suite gap rather than an equivalent mutant.

name.text: Why deleted transitions are easy to kill

questiontext.text: Why is a delete-transition mutant usually easy to kill once its transition is exercised?

answer.text: The run cannot continue, ending the trace in ⊥, which differs from the base's output at that point

feedback.text: Correct — the stuck run yields ⊥, an immediate observable difference.

answer.text: Because deletion adds a new state that the base lacks

feedback.text: Deletion removes a transition; it does not add a state.

answer.text: Because deletion changes the initial state

feedback.text: The initial state is unchanged by a transition deletion.

answer.text: It is never killable

feedback.text: It is killed by any test that reaches the deleted transition.

generalfeedback.text: Any test that reaches the deleted transition produces ⊥ instead of the base's output — an immediate distinguishing difference.

name.text: Traces for the q1-a output mutant on aa

questiontext.text: For the mutant that makes q1-a output 1 instead of 0, running aa gives which comparison?

answer.text: Base "01" vs mutant "11" — they differ at the first output, so aa kills it

feedback.text: Correct — q1-a now emits 1, changing the first symbol.

answer.text: Base "11" vs mutant "01"

feedback.text: The base emits 0 first (its q1-a output is 0); the mutant emits 1.

answer.text: Both give "01" — it survives

feedback.text: The mutant emits 1 at the first step, so its trace is "11".

answer.text: Both give "11"

feedback.text: The base's q1-a output is 0, so the base trace is "01".

generalfeedback.text: On "aa" the base yields "01" and the q1-a-output mutant yields "11"; the difference at position 1 kills it.

name.text: What a retarget-killing test must do

questiontext.text: A retarget mutant sends q2-a to a different state but keeps its output. For a test to kill it, the test must:

answer.text: Continue past that transition until the different destination causes a different output symbol; a differing state alone is not observable

feedback.text: Correct — only a divergent output makes the difference visible.

answer.text: Simply reach the retargeted transition once

feedback.text: Reaching it is not enough if the emitted outputs still match.

answer.text: Have the same length as the FSM's state count

feedback.text: Length matters only insofar as it exposes an output difference, not as a fixed count.

answer.text: End immediately after the retargeted transition

feedback.text: Stopping there hides the difference, since the retarget keeps the same output.

generalfeedback.text: Killing is defined by output traces, so a retarget (which keeps the transition's output) is only exposed when a later input yields a different output from the new destination.

questiontext.text: A model-mutant survived the suite. The two possible explanations are:

answer.text: The suite is too weak to reach or distinguish the mutation, or the mutant is equivalent (no test can ever kill it)

feedback.text: Correct — a survivor is a suite gap or an equivalent mutant.

answer.text: The base model is defective, or the suite ran too fast

feedback.text: Neither speed nor a base defect explains a survivor.

answer.text: It is always an equivalent mutant

feedback.text: Many survivors are fixable suite gaps, not equivalent.

answer.text: It is always a suite gap

feedback.text: Some survivors are genuinely equivalent and unkillable.

generalfeedback.text: Distinguishing the two — suite gap vs equivalent — requires human analysis; only the gap is fixable by adding tests.

questiontext.text: "Remove the q2-a transition entirely" is which operator?

answer.text: Delete

feedback.text: Correct — the transition is removed.

answer.text: Retarget

feedback.text: Retarget keeps the transition but changes its target.

answer.text: Output change

feedback.text: Output change keeps the transition and alters its emitted symbol.

answer.text: Guard negation

feedback.text: The explorer has no guard operator; removing a transition is delete.

generalfeedback.text: Removing a transition outright is the delete operator (mutant M1 deletes q2-a).

questiontext.text: How do you tell a suite-gap survivor from an equivalent survivor?

answer.text: A gap survivor is killable by some test that covers or distinguishes the mutation; an equivalent survivor cannot be killed by any test

feedback.text: Correct — killability is what separates the two.

answer.text: A gap survivor is unkillable; an equivalent one is killable

feedback.text: This is reversed: the gap is killable, the equivalent is not.

answer.text: Both are killable by the same single test

feedback.text: An equivalent mutant is killable by no test at all.

answer.text: You compare their state counts

feedback.text: State counts do not distinguish gaps from equivalents.

generalfeedback.text: Adding a covering test kills a gap survivor; no test can ever kill an equivalent mutant, because its behaviour matches the base.

name.text: Why the q2-a→q1 mutant survives the suite

questiontext.text: The mutant retargeting q2-a to q1 (instead of q3) survives the suite, yet it is not equivalent. Why?

answer.text: The suite's sequences are too short to reach an input where landing in q1 vs q3 yields a different output — a suite gap, so a longer test could kill it

feedback.text: Correct — the difference only shows on a longer input.

answer.text: q1 and q3 are behaviourally identical, so it can never be killed

feedback.text: q1 and q3 are distinguishable (e.g. by "aa"), so it is not equivalent.

answer.text: The retarget operator never changes behaviour

feedback.text: Retarget can change behaviour; here it does, just not within the suite.

answer.text: The mutant failed to build

feedback.text: It builds fine; it simply is not distinguished by these tests.

generalfeedback.text: q1 and q3 differ, so the mutant is killable, but only by an input long enough to expose the difference — the suite lacks such a test.

questiontext.text: In this Mealy-FSM setting, killing a mutant strictly means:

answer.text: Finding a test whose output trace on the mutant differs from the base's output trace

feedback.text: Correct — killing is defined by a divergent output trace.

answer.text: Reaching a different state than the base, regardless of outputs

feedback.text: A differing internal state is not observable; only outputs count.

answer.text: Producing a longer trace than the base

feedback.text: Trace length is not the criterion; a differing symbol is.

answer.text: Visiting more states than the base

feedback.text: State visits are internal; killing requires an output difference.

generalfeedback.text: evalMutant compares output traces; a mutant is killed only when some test's output trace differs from the base's.

questiontext.text: The explorer's adjusted mutation score differs from the raw score by:

answer.text: Excluding equivalent mutants from the denominator, since they can never be killed

feedback.text: Correct — adjusted = killed / (total − equivalent).

answer.text: Excluding killed mutants from the numerator

feedback.text: Killed mutants remain in the numerator; equivalents leave the denominator.

answer.text: Counting only delete mutants

feedback.text: All operators count; only equivalents are excluded.

answer.text: Doubling the raw score

feedback.text: The adjustment removes equivalents, not a doubling.

generalfeedback.text: The adjusted score removes equivalent mutants from the total so they do not unfairly depress the measure.

questiontext.text: On the base model, the output trace for input ab is:

feedback.text: Correct — q1-a emits 0 into q2, then q2-b emits 1.
That is the trace for "ba", not "ab".
That is a length-3 trace (e.g. "aaa"); "ab" has two inputs.
Both transitions exist in the base, so there is no ⊥.

questiontext.text: Which pairing of a term with its role is correct?

answer.text: "killed" = the suite distinguished the mutant's output trace from the base's

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly what killed means.

answer.text: "survived" = the suite distinguished the mutant from the base

feedback.text: Distinguishing means killed; surviving means not distinguished.

answer.text: "equivalent" = the mutant has fewer states than the base

feedback.text: Equivalent means identical behaviour, not fewer states.

answer.text: "⊥" = the model reached its initial state

feedback.text: ⊥ marks a missing transition (stuck run), not the initial state.

generalfeedback.text: Killed = distinguished; survived = not distinguished; equivalent = behaviourally identical (unkillable); ⊥ = stuck at a missing transition.

questiontext.text: The mutant retargeting q2-a from q3 to q4 is marked equivalent because:

answer.text: States q3 and q4 are behaviourally identical, so sending q2-a to q4 instead of q3 never changes any output

name.text: Does a 100% model score guarantee code adequacy

answer.text: No — the model abstracts away code-level detail, so a model-adequate suite can still miss faults in the implementation's code

feedback.text: Correct — model adequacy does not imply code-branch adequacy.

answer.text: Yes — model adequacy always implies code adequacy

feedback.text: The model omits code detail, so this implication does not hold.

answer.text: Yes — because both techniques use mutation operators

feedback.text: Sharing the mutation idea does not make the abstraction levels equivalent.

answer.text: No — because model mutation cannot generate tests

feedback.text: It can drive test design; the real reason is the abstraction gap.

generalfeedback.text: A killed model-mutant proves the suite distinguishes model behaviours, not that it covers code branches — model mutation works at a higher abstraction than code mutation.

questiontext.text: In the explorer's framing, a killed model-mutant proves that the suite:

answer.text: Distinguishes model behaviours — not that it covers the implementation's code branches

feedback.text: Correct — killing is about behavioural distinction at the model level.

answer.text: Covers every branch in the source code

answer.text: Achieves 100% statement coverage

answer.text: Contains no equivalent mutants

feedback.text: Killing one mutant says nothing about whether others are equivalent.

name.text: Why the delete mutant's trace ends in ⊥

answer.text: The delete operator changes the first output symbol to ⊥

name.text: Why exclude the equivalent mutant from the score

questiontext.text: Why does the explorer report an adjusted score that excludes the equivalent mutant?

answer.text: An equivalent mutant is unkillable by definition, so counting it would unfairly depress the adequacy measure

questiontext.text: A key trade-off of model-level versus code-level mutation is that model mutation:

answer.text: Works at a higher abstraction — it can expose design/spec-level test gaps early, but a high model score does not guarantee code-branch coverage, and equivalent mutants still arise

feedback.text: Correct — higher abstraction brings both an advantage and limitations.

answer.text: Is strictly more powerful than code mutation in every respect

feedback.text: It is not strictly superior; it abstracts away code detail.

feedback.text: Equivalent mutants still arise (e.g. q2-a→q4).

feedback.text: It runs on the model, needing no source code.

generalfeedback.text: Model mutation catches behavioural test gaps at the model level and needs no source, but its score does not imply code-branch adequacy and equivalent mutants remain a challenge.
